subject: community-medicine
title: Emerging infections, hospital infections and antimicrobial resistance

steps.tx: The **International Health Regulations** (IHR) oblige countries to notify WHO of certain events. Immediately notifiable diseases are **smallpox, human influenza, wild polio and SARS**. Cholera, plague and yellow fever are also notifiable. HIV/AIDS is not covered by the IHR, and this is a frequent exam trap.

steps.tx: A **Public Health Emergency of International Concern** (PHEIC) is declared by WHO under the IHR when an event is serious, unusual and spreads across borders. COVID-19 was declared a PHEIC on 30 January 2020 and called a pandemic on 11 March 2020. WHO named the disease COVID-19 on 11 February 2020.

steps.tx: **Hospital acquired infections** (nosocomial) develop after at least **48 hours** of hospitalisation, and *Staphylococcus aureus* is the commonest cause. Hand contact is the most common transmission route, so **hand hygiene** is the single most important preventive measure. Alcohol hand rub is preferred unless hands are visibly soiled, when soap and water is needed.

steps.tx: The split photo teaches the single most important ward habit. On one side hands are rubbed with alcohol using the accepted hand hygiene technique beside a wall dispenser. On the other side lathered hands go under a running tap for **visibly soiled** hands. The captions name this choice the key step against **nosocomial** spread since hand contact carries organisms between patients. Learners should recall **alcohol rub** as routine and soap plus water when dirt is seen.
steps.say: Compare the two halves before answering. Alcohol rub suits routine ward contact and follows a set rubbing technique. Soap and water is required when hands look dirty. Hand contact is the commonest route for hospital acquired infection, so correct hand hygiene prevents more cases than any other single step. Pick the method by looking at the hands first.

steps.tx: **Antimicrobial resistance** (AMR) is worsened by overuse of antibiotics. Extensive vancomycin prophylaxis has led to vancomycin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*. MRSA control focuses on preventing hand transfer, not on giving vancomycin to all patients. India's **Kayakalp** initiative, launched in 2015, rewards hospital hygiene and environmental sanitation.
